title: kubectl Essentials
summary: Command syntax, output formats, imperative vs declarative management, generating manifests and switching contexts.

blocks.text: Your radio to the front desk (`kubectl`) uses one fixed call pattern: action, cargo type, name, extras. Say the type loosely (`pods`, `pod` or `po` all work), but spell names exactly. Leave out the name and you mean every item of that type. Extras you say on air beat the defaults. The radio reads its settings from a codebook in your home folder unless you point it elsewhere, and `kubectl api-resources` reads out every type and its nickname.
kubectl talks to the control plane through the Kubernetes API. Every command follows one shape:
kubectl [command] [TYPE] [NAME] [flags]

items: **command**: the operation, such as `create`, `get`, `describe` or `delete`.
**TYPE**: the resource type. It is case-insensitive and accepts singular, plural or short forms, so `kubectl get pod <name>`, `kubectl get pods <name>` and `kubectl get po <name>` are equivalent.
**NAME**: case-sensitive. Leave it out to act on every resource of that type (`kubectl get pods`).
**flags**: optional. A flag on the command line beats default values and matching environment variables.
Several objects at once: `TYPE1 name1 name2` (same type), `TYPE1/name1 TYPE1/name2 TYPE2/name3` (mixed types) or `-f <file>` (repeatable).
By default kubectl reads `config` in `$HOME/.kube`. Point it elsewhere with the `KUBECONFIG` variable or `--kubeconfig`.

blocks.text: `kubectl api-resources` prints every resource type with its short names, API version, kind and whether it is namespaced.

The front desk normally answers in plain speech. Ask for a different report format with `-o`: `wide` adds columns like which ship a bay sits on, `yaml` or `json` reads back the whole form, `jsonpath` or `custom-columns` picks just the fields you want, and `name` gives only names. You can sort the list, filter by field, or keep the line open (`-w`). A quick list (`get`) is short; a full briefing (`describe`) may take several calls.
Plain human-readable text is the default. Add `-o` (or `--output`) to change it.

rows: Plain text plus extra columns; for Pods that includes the node name
Only the fields selected by a JSONPath expression
A table of columns you define, e.g. `NAME:.metadata.name`

items: Sort a list with `--sort-by=<jsonpath_exp>`, e.g. `kubectl get pods --sort-by=.metadata.name`.
`-w` / `--watch` on `get` keeps streaming updates to the object.
`get` lists objects of one type; `describe` builds a richer view (for a node it adds its Pods and events) and may make several API calls.
Filter by field: `kubectl get pods --field-selector=spec.nodeName=<node-name>`.

blocks.text: There are three ways to place orders. Shout one over the radio (imperative command): fast, but nothing is written down. Hand over a form and say "create" or "replace" (imperative config): `replace` swaps the whole order, wiping anything changed since. Or drop a folder of forms in the tray (`kubectl apply`): the desk works out what to add, change or remove, touching only the differences. Preview with `kubectl diff`. Pick one way per order; mixing them causes chaos.

items: Imperative commands are the quickest way to start or do a one-off task, but they leave no record of earlier configuration and no template for the next object.
`replace` swaps in the whole spec from the file. Anything changed on the live object but missing from the file is lost.
`apply` works out per object whether to create, patch or delete. It writes only the differences, so changes from other writers survive.
Preview first with `kubectl diff -f configs/`, then `kubectl apply -f configs/`. Add `-R` to recurse into subdirectories.

blocks.text: Pick one technique per object. Mixing techniques on the same object gives undefined behavior.

Nobody at the port writes forms from memory. Ask the front desk for a blank, pre-filled draft without sending anything (`--dry-run=client -o yaml`), save it, fix the fields you need, then file it with `kubectl apply -f`. Unsure what a box means? The form guide (`kubectl explain`) tells you. Forms can be YAML or JSON, and you can even read one straight over the radio (`apply -f -`). On a timed exam, this habit saves you.
Rather than typing YAML from memory, let kubectl write a starting manifest, edit it, then apply it.

kubectl run <pod-name> --image=<image> --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml
kubectl create deployment <name> --image=<image>
kubectl create job <name> --image=<image> -- <command>
kubectl expose rc <name> --port=<port> --target-port=<target-port>
kubectl explain pods   # field docs for Pod manifests

Time is tight in the CKA. Generate a skeleton with `--dry-run=client -o yaml > <file>.yaml`, fix the fields you need, then `kubectl apply -f <file>.yaml`. Use `kubectl explain` instead of guessing field names.

items: Manifests may be YAML or JSON with `.yaml`, `.yml` or `.json` extensions.
`kubectl apply -f -` reads a manifest from stdin, handy with a heredoc.
The quick reference calls `apply` the recommended way to manage applications in production.

sections.heading: kubeconfig files and contexts
sections.sourceTitle: Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files

blocks.text: Your radio carries a codebook (kubeconfig) listing ports, staff identities, yards and passwords. A preset channel (context) bundles one port, one yard and one identity, and the radio uses the current preset unless told otherwise. You can stack several codebooks (`KUBECONFIG`); the first book to set an entry wins. Name one book (`--kubeconfig`) and the radio reads only that. Only load codebooks you trust: a crafted one can run harmful code.
A **kubeconfig** file holds clusters, users, namespaces and authentication details. The name is generic: no file actually has to be called kubeconfig.

items: A **context** names a combination of **cluster**, **namespace** and **user**. kubectl uses the current context unless told otherwise.
`KUBECONFIG` lists files to merge: colon-separated on Linux and Mac, semicolon-separated on Windows. If it is unset, kubectl uses `$HOME/.kube/config`.
`--kubeconfig` uses only that one file and skips merging.
When merging, the first file to set a value or map key wins, and later files never change it.
Context choice: the `--context` flag first, otherwise `current-context` from the merged config.
Paths inside a kubeconfig are relative to that file; paths on the command line are relative to the working directory.

blocks.text: Only use kubeconfig files you trust. A crafted file can run malicious code or expose files.

Before giving orders, check which port your radio is tuned to. `kubectl config get-contexts` lists your preset channels, `current-context` shows the one in use, and `use-context` switches. You can also set a default yard for the current preset. On the exam, switch to the named channel first and confirm it: sending perfect orders to the wrong port earns nothing. Need every yard at once? Add `-A`.

kubectl config view                      # merged settings
kubectl config get-contexts              # list contexts
kubectl config current-context           # show current one
kubectl config use-context <context>     # switch
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<namespace>
When a task names a context, run `kubectl config use-context <context>` before anything else and confirm with `kubectl config current-context`. Working in the wrong cluster costs the whole task.

items: `--all-namespaces` has the shorthand `-A`, e.g. `kubectl get pods -A`.
`kubectl config view --raw` also shows certificate data and secrets.

blocks.text: Seasoned dock hands keep radio shortcuts: a short call sign (`alias k=kubectl`) and auto-complete. They listen to a container's chatter (`logs -f`), even from its previous run (`--previous`), step inside it (`exec`), run a private line from their desk to a bay (`port-forward`), tag bays, resize a contract (`scale`), undo a bad upgrade (`rollout undo`), and check the gauges (`top`). Turning up radio detail (`--v=6`, `--v=8`) reveals exactly what was sent.

alias k=kubectl
source <(kubectl completion bash)
kubectl logs -f <pod>                     # stream logs
kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous
kubectl exec --stdin --tty <pod> -- /bin/sh
kubectl port-forward <pod> <local-port>:<pod-port>
kubectl label pods <pod> <key>=<value>
kubectl scale --replicas=<n> deployment/<name>
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>
kubectl delete pod <pod> --now           # no grace period
kubectl get pods --show-labels
kubectl top pod

items: `--previous` shows logs from the earlier instance of a restarted container.
`kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Running` lists only running Pods.
`kubectl events --types=Warning` lists warning events.
Verbosity: `-v` / `--v` from 0 upward; `--v=6` shows requested resources and `--v=8` shows HTTP request contents.

flashcards.front: General syntax of a kubectl command?

flashcards.back: TYPE is case-insensitive (singular, plural or short form). NAME is case-sensitive.

flashcards.back: Imperative commands, imperative object configuration (create/replace -f), declarative object configuration (apply -f).

questions.stem: Which three commands produce the same result?

options.text: kubectl get pod <name>, kubectl get pods <name>, kubectl get po <name>
options.explanation: TYPE accepts singular, plural and short forms.

options.text: kubectl get pod <name>, kubectl describe pod <name>, kubectl logs <name>
options.explanation: These are different operations with different output.

options.text: kubectl get pods, kubectl get pods -A, kubectl get pods -o wide
options.explanation: -A widens the scope to all namespaces and -o wide adds columns.

options.text: kubectl get svc, kubectl get sa, kubectl get sts
options.explanation: These are services, service accounts and StatefulSets: different types.

questions.stem: You need to see which node each Pod runs on, in the usual table layout. Which flag?

options.explanation: Wide output adds columns; for Pods it includes the node name.
Prints only resource names.
Streams updates; it doesn't add the node column.
This turns off server-side columns, giving less detail.

questions.stem: Which are valid kubectl output formats? Select 3.

options.explanation: Prints the fields picked by a JSONPath expression.
Prints a table of columns you define.
Prints the full object as YAML.
A real flag, but it sorts lists; it is not an output format.

questions.stem: A teammate changed a live object by hand. You then run kubectl replace -f with an older file that lacks that change. What happens?

options.text: The change is lost because replace overwrites the spec with the file
options.explanation: replace drops anything missing from the configuration file.

options.text: The change is kept because replace only patches differences
options.explanation: That describes apply, which uses patch.

options.text: kubectl refuses to run until the file is updated
options.explanation: There is no such check.

options.text: The object is deleted and must be created again
options.explanation: replace updates the object; it doesn't leave it deleted.

questions.stem: Which technique detects create, patch and delete operations per object and works well on directories?

options.text: Declarative object configuration with kubectl apply
options.explanation: apply works out the operation per object.

options.text: Imperative commands such as kubectl create deployment
options.explanation: These act on live objects and you choose the operation.

options.text: Imperative object configuration with kubectl create -f
options.explanation: You name the operation and it works best on single files.
diff only previews changes; it doesn't create, patch or delete anything.

questions.stem: It is safe to manage the same object with kubectl create, kubectl replace and kubectl apply interchangeably.

options.explanation: Mixing techniques on one object is explicitly undefined behavior.
Correct. Stick to one management technique per object.

questions.stem: Which command writes a Pod manifest to a file without creating the Pod?

options.explanation: Client dry-run prints the object instead of sending it.
Without --dry-run the Pod is actually created.

options.text: kubectl get pod nginx -o yaml > pod.yaml
options.explanation: This exports an existing Pod; it doesn't generate a new one.
explain prints field documentation, not a manifest.

questions.stem: You can't remember the fields allowed in a Pod spec. Which command shows them?

options.explanation: explain prints documentation for a resource's manifest fields.
describe shows the state of existing Pods.
Lists resource types, not their fields.
Compares a file with the live object.

questions.stem: KUBECONFIG lists two files and both define current-context. Which value does kubectl use?

options.text: The value from the first file in the list
options.explanation: The first file to set a value wins; later files never change it.

options.text: The value from the last file in the list
options.explanation: Later files don't override earlier ones.

options.text: kubectl fails with a conflict error
options.explanation: Conflicting authentication techniques fail, but duplicate keys follow first-wins.
The default file is used only when KUBECONFIG is unset.

questions.stem: Which three parameters make up a kubeconfig context? Select 3.

options.explanation: Part of every context.
Part of every context.
Part of every context.
proxy-url is set on a cluster entry, not as a context parameter.

questions.stem: When --kubeconfig is set, kubectl still merges in the files listed in KUBECONFIG.

options.explanation: With --kubeconfig, only that file is used and nothing is merged.
Correct. The flag means one file, no merging.

questions.stem: A task asks you to work in namespace <namespace> for all following commands in your current context. Which command?

options.explanation: Saves the namespace into the current context.
use-context switches contexts, not namespaces.
Creates a namespace but doesn't make it the default.
Sets a cluster entry in the kubeconfig.

questions.stem: A container keeps restarting. Which command shows the logs of the instance that crashed?

options.explanation: --previous shows the earlier instance of the container.
Streams the current instance's logs.
Attaches to the running container.
Shows CPU and memory usage.

questions.stem: Which commands are imperative (they act directly on live objects without a manifest file)? Select 2.

options.explanation: Creates the object straight from flags.
Changes the live object from flags.
apply is driven by a manifest file.
diff compares a file to the cluster and changes nothing.
